title: Torque on a Current Loop: Motors and Meters
lead: A straight wire carrying a current across a magnetic field is pushed sideways. Bend that wire into a loop, hang the loop on a shaft, and the pushes on its two sides are still equal and opposite, so the loop goes nowhere, but they no longer act along the same line, so the loop turns: that is a motor, and the torque it feels is the number of turns times the current times the area of the loop times the field strength times the sine of the angle between the field and the perpendicular to the loop. The torque is greatest when the loop lies edge on to the field, falls to zero when the loop faces the field squarely, and reverses once the loop has passed that position, so a motor keeps turning only because switches called brushes reverse the current there twice a revolution. Shape the poles of the magnet so that the field crosses the loop squarely wherever the loop stands, hang a spring on the shaft, and the same three parts make a meter whose needle deflects in proportion to the current.
objectives: Describe how motors and meters work in terms of torque on a current loop.
Calculate the torque on a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field.
summary_html: • The torque $\ktau$ on a current-carrying loop of any shape in a uniform magnetic field. is $\ktau = N\kIcur A\kBmag\sin\theta ,$ where $N$ is the number of turns, $\kIcur$ is the current, $A$ is the area of the loop, $\kBmag$ is the magnetic field strength, and $\theta$ is the angle between the perpendicular to the loop and the magnetic field.
notes: The four problems the book leaves unkeyed are left out: the maximum torque on a 150-turn square loop and its torque at 10.9°, the field strength a 200-turn loop would need for a torque of 300 N⋅m, the three angles at which the torque is 90.0, 50.0 and 10.0 percent of its maximum, and the 200-turn circular loop lying in Earth’s field. Nothing else in the module is left out: all four of its drawings are redrawn as interactive figures with the book’s own images beside them, the loop on its shaft, the four top views and the brushes being one figure because they are one machine drawn three times. Example 22.5 prints the area of a loop 10.0 cm on a side as 0.100 m², where the arithmetic of the line and its answer of 30.0 N⋅m both take it as 0.0100 m²; the line is kept as the book sets it.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 22.33) Torque on a current loop. A current-carrying loop of wire attached to a vertically rotating shaft feels magnetic forces that produce a clockwise torque as viewed from above. (Figure 22.34) Top views of a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field. (a) The equation for torque is derived using this view. Note that the perpendicular to the loop makes an angle θ with the field that is the same as the angle between w/2 and F. (b) The maximum torque occurs when θ is a right angle and sin θ = 1. (c) Zero (minimum) torque occurs when θ is zero and sin θ = 0. (d) The torque reverses once the loop rotates past θ = 0. (Figure 22.35) (a) As the angular momentum of the coil carries it through θ = 0, the brushes reverse the current to keep the torque clockwise. (b) The coil will rotate continuously in the clockwise direction, with the current reversing each half revolution to maintain the clockwise torque.

Meters are very similar to motors but only rotate through a part of a revolution. The magnetic poles of this meter are shaped to keep the component of B perpendicular to the loop constant, so that the torque does not depend on θ and the deflection against the return spring is proportional only to the current I.

exercises.prompt: Draw a diagram and use RHR-1 to show that the forces on the top and bottom segments of the motor’s current loop in Figure 22.33 are vertical and produce no torque about the axis of rotation.

answer.solution: Draw the loop as the book draws it, with the field running from the north pole on the left to the south pole on the right, the current coming up the near side of the loop, across the top from left to right, and down the far side. Take the top segment first. Its current runs across the loop, at some angle to the field but always in the horizontal plane. Lay the thumb of the right hand along that current and the fingers along the field, and the perpendicular to the palm points straight up. So the force on the top segment is vertical. Now take the bottom segment. Its current runs the other way across the loop, since the current has gone round, so the same rule turns the force over and it points straight down. The two forces are therefore equal in size, opposite in direction, and both parallel to the shaft. They give no net force, because they cancel. They give no torque either, because a torque needs a lever arm perpendicular to the force: a force that runs along the axis of rotation has none, and turning the loop about the shaft does not move the point where either force acts any nearer to or further from that axis. All the turning comes from the two vertical sides, whose forces are horizontal and act at a distance w/2 from the shaft on either side of it.

exercises.prompt: (a) By how many percent is the torque of a motor decreased if its permanent magnets lose 5.0% of their strength? (b) How many percent would the current need to be increased to return the torque to original values?

parts.hint: The torque goes with the field strength and with nothing else that has changed, so the fraction the field loses is the fraction the torque loses.
The current has to make up the whole of the lost factor, so it must be multiplied by 1/0.950.

answer.solution:
(a) $\ktau$ decreases by 5.00% if B decreases by 5.00%
(b) 5.26% increase

exercises.prompt: Find the current through a loop needed to create a maximum torque of $9\text{.}\text{00 N}\cdot\text{m.}$ The loop has 50 square turns that are 15.0 cm on a side and is in a uniform 0.800-T magnetic field.

answer.hint: The torque is at its maximum, so the sine is 1; solve $\ktau_{\text{max}} = N\kIcur A\kBmag$ for the current, taking the area as the side squared.

exercises.prompt: Since the equation for torque on a current-carrying loop is $\ktau = N\kIcur A\kBmag\sin\theta$, the units of $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ must equal units of $\text{A}\cdot{\text{m}}^{2}\;\text{T}$. Verify this.

A proton has a magnetic field due to its spin on its axis. The field is similar to that created by a circular current loop $0\text{.}\text{650}\times {\text{10}}^{-\text{15}}\;\text{m}$ in radius with a current of $1\text{.}\text{05}\times {\text{10}}^{4}\;\text{A}$ (no kidding). Find the maximum torque on a proton in a 2.50-T field. (This is a significant torque on a small particle.)

answer.hint: The loop has one turn and the torque is at its maximum, so it is the current times the area of the circle times the field; the area is $\pi r^2$ with the radius as given.

exercises.prompt: Repeat the problem the book prints before this one — “(a) A 200-turn circular loop of radius 50.0 cm is vertical, with its axis on an east-west line. A current of 100 A circulates clockwise in the loop when viewed from the east. The Earth’s field here is due north, parallel to the ground, with a strength of $3\text{.}\text{00}\times {\text{10}}^{-5}\;\text{T}$. What are the direction and magnitude of the torque on the loop? (b) Does this device have any practical applications as a motor?” — but with the loop lying flat on the ground with its current circulating counterclockwise (when viewed from above) in a location where the Earth’s field is north, but at an angle $\text{45}\text{.}0^\circ$ below the horizontal and with a strength of $\text{6.}\text{00}\times {\text{10}}^{-5}\;\text{T}$.

answer.hint: The loop lies flat, so the perpendicular to it is vertical and the angle between that perpendicular and a field tilted 45.0° below the horizontal is 45.0°; the area is $\pi r^2$.
answer.solution:
(a) $\text{0.666 N}\cdot\text{m}$ west
(b) This is not a very significant torque, so practical use would be limited. Also, the current would need to be alternated to make the loop rotate (otherwise it would oscillate).
